cells.tense: Right now you are holding a living pattern and handing it over without losing it.
cells.ask: Take one thing you know and explain it to someone in a way that fits their life, not yours. Then watch what they do with it and let that tell you what to keep.
cells.core:
You've got a way of seeing that's still working, and you're passing it on without freezing it. You can hold the shape of something long enough to hand it over, and you adjust it for whoever's on the other end instead of insisting on the original words. That's why it lands — people pick up what you carry because you deliver it in their language.

The test is whether the shape stays. Teach something to one person, in a form that fits their world, and watch what happens when they use it. If they can carry it further than you did, the pattern is alive. If it comes back rigid or thin, the transmission has gone stiff. That's what tuning means here: you keep adjusting the shape until it moves on its own in someone else's hands.
cells.sheetLine: You pass on what you know so it stays useful in other hands.
cells.verb: carrying a way of seeing forward so it survives translation and use
cells.place: at a remove where the shape shows and the surface doesn't

cells.tense: You are already guarding a shape from a future where no one holds it right.
cells.ask: Say what you know once, in the plainest words you have, then let someone else repeat it back wrong. See if the shape survives their version before you correct it.
cells.core:
You can read the pattern beautifully, but somewhere in your head there's a future where nobody gets it right, so you start closing windows before anyone's even reached for one. The shape gets locked into the letter — the exact words, the proper order, the only acceptable version. The thing you're protecting stops being a living way of seeing and turns into a wall.

The pattern doesn't need you to defend it from use. It needs one clean pass where you say what you know in plain words and then let it go into someone else's mouth. If it comes back wrong, that's not damage — that's the shape working. What you're guarding can survive being handed over badly, and that's the only way you ever find out.
cells.sheetLine: You've gone from carrying the pattern to guarding its exact wording.
cells.verb: carrying a way of seeing forward so it survives translation and use
cells.place: at a remove where the shape shows and the surface doesn't

cells.tense: You are standing without a shared frame, and the shape you can make out has nowhere to go.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've worked out alone and write the shape under it in plain words, simply enough that another person could repeat it back to you.
cells.core:
You can make out the shape, but there's nothing around to hand it to, so it sits. With no working way to pass it on, each idea starts over from nothing — you rebuild what you worked out before, and it doesn't gain the weight that comes from being used by someone else. The clarity holds. The move forward stopped.

A frame you can put words to would give it somewhere to go. Take one pattern you've figured out alone and write it plainly enough for someone else to say back. That's the move — not finding a group first, just making the shape sayable in a form another person could pick up. Once it's sayable, there's something to put in someone's hands.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the pattern, but you're not passing it on.
cells.verb: carrying a way of seeing forward so it survives translation and use

cells.tense: You are teaching while telling yourself you are only thinking out loud.
cells.ask: Name one thing you keep saying to people and call it a way of seeing you picked, not just an observation. Then say where you got it from.
cells.core:
It happens in how you explain things, what you notice, how you fold a pattern into plain language so someone else can hold it. People take things from you. But if asked, you'd say you're just thinking out loud, just making an observation, nothing special being passed along. Words are moving. Your name isn't on them.

Something is doing that passing, and it isn't an accident. You keep choosing which shapes to put into other people's hands and how to say them so they land. That choice is yours, and so is the source — where you got it doesn't have to be original for the passing along to be yours. Calling it a way of seeing you picked is what puts it in your hands.
cells.sheetLine: People are learning from you and you haven't called it that.

attempts.check: The record says Culture transmits but does not settle whether this person has a community at all; the reader might say there is no one around to carry anything to, and the ask would still stand since it asks for the frame, not an audience. The two lines that would flatter me more than serve them are 'people already learn from you' and 'the pattern is yours' — both claim more than the draw supports, since authorship may be shared or borrowed and visible teaching may not be happening. The ask survives a wrong read because it gives one small way to test whether the shape holds; if it doesn't, the shape is what fails, not the person.
